ddx.step1_summary:
• Chief complaint: 2-day history of lower abdominal ("lower tummy") pain.
• Associated symptoms: feels "hot and sweaty"; mild nausea (no vomiting); slight pink-tinged urine (gross hematuria); ↑ urinary frequency; increased thirst; constipation last week but now normal; no dysuria, no back/flank pain, no diarrhoea, no upper-abdominal or reflux symptoms, no vaginal discharge or abnormal bleeding.
• Onset/duration: began ~48 h ago, constant location described as mid-lower abdomen.
• Aggravating/alleviating factors: none specified.
• Past medical history: none significant.
• Medications/allergies: no regular meds; amoxicillin allergy; had contraceptive implant removed 1 yr ago.
• Family history: mother – early breast cancer.
• Social history: lives with parents; non-smoker; drinks ~1 beer on 4 days/week; no recent travel.
• Vital signs & exam: only temperature checked at home, 37 °C; no physical exam data provided.
• Labs/imaging: none performed/mentioned.

V: Urolithiasis (renal or ureteric stone): can cause hematuria, lower abdominal discomfort, nausea.
Renal vein thrombosis: much less likely but could present with hematuria and pain.
I: Acute uncomplicated cystitis: suprapubic pain, frequency, hematuria, low-grade or absent fever.
Early pyelonephritis: UTI spectrum; would expect flank pain/fever but could be evolving.
Appendicitis: classically migrates from mid-abdomen to RLQ; early stage may be mid-abdominal with low-grade symptoms.
N: Bladder carcinoma: painless hematuria but possible suprapubic discomfort; age makes this unlikely.
Ovarian neoplasm with torsion/bleeding: could mimic lower abdominal pain.
D: Diverticulitis: left-lower pain, low-grade fever, bowel habit change.
Inflammatory bowel disease flare: abdominal pain, occasional blood, systemic symptoms.
I2: Drug-induced cystitis (e.g., cyclophosphamide) – not on such meds.
Alcohol-related gastritis mimicking pain – location atypical.
C: Congenital urinary tract anomaly predisposing to infection (e.g., vesicoureteral reflux).
A: Interstitial cystitis/painful bladder syndrome: suprapubic pain, frequency, negative cultures.
T: Minor abdominal/urinary tract trauma causing hematuria – no trauma reported.
E: Early pregnancy-related issue (e.g., ectopic) – lower abdominal pain; needs pregnancy ruled out.
Metabolic ketoacidosis (DKA) – thirst, frequency, nausea, but would expect polyuria & systemic illness.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Acute uncomplicated cystitis (lower urinary tract infection)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic triad of suprapubic pain, urinary frequency, and visible hematuria in a young woman with minimal systemic features strongly suggests cystitis.
supporting_evidence: Female sex, sexually active age group
No flank pain (argues for lower vs upper UTI)
opposing_evidence: Thirst sweats could imply systemic process, but not specific

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Microscopic or gross hematuria with abdominal pain and nausea could signal a calculus, even without classical colicky flank pain if stone is distal.
supporting_evidence: Lower abdominal discomfort possible with distal ureter or bladder stone
opposing_evidence: Pain described as mild, central—not severe colicky or flank-to-groin radiation
No restlessness or acute distress typical of renal colic
Frequency more typical of cystitis than stones

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Early appendicitis can present with mid-abdominal pain and mild nausea before localising; sweating/low-grade fever fit but urinary findings are atypical.
opposing_evidence: Pain has not migrated to right iliac fossa
Presence of hematuria & frequency not explained

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Lower abdominal pain in a young woman must raise PID consideration, but urinary blood/frequency and absent vaginal discharge make it less likely.
supporting_evidence: Lower abdominal pain, mild systemic symptoms
opposing_evidence: No dyspareunia, no history of STI risk discussed
